question: In June 2023, the Italian Government decided that the ‘pleasure and cruise port of Fiumicino Isola Sacra’ was a strategic project under the ‘reception of pilgrims and visitors’ subsection of the Rome 2025 Jubilee programme. A full environmental authorisation process had already been completed for the project, although this did not include its newly added function of receiving cruise ships.
The project has indeed been overhauled to enable the port to welcome cruise ships – thus reducing its function as a pleasure port by 50% – such as Oasis-class vessels, the largest in the world.

This will have a cascade of cumulative effects on existing ports or those under construction nearby, firstly impacting an area with incalculable artistic, archaeological, cultural-identity and historical riches, including the archaeological heritage of the Roman remains and the ancient village of Ostia as well as the nearby lighthouse and the traditional ‘trabucco’ fishing techniques in use in the area.

The project may also pose risks to the environment since it is located within the Natura 2000 network, encroaching on three special conservation areas and adjacent to a site of Community importance. Can the Commission therefore say: 1.

Whether it believes that building the planned port in Fiumicino Isola Sacra would breach the principles of preserving and safeguarding the cultural heritage enshrined in Article 3 of the TEU and Article 167 of the TFEU?
Whether it believes it could constitute a breach of the ‘Habitats Directive’ – Directive 92/43/EEC on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora?
answer: The primary responsibility for the protection of cultural heritage lies with the Member States, as stipulated in Articles 6 and 167 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).

While the EU ‘shall ensure that Europe's cultural heritage is safeguarded’ (Article 3 of the Treaty on the European Union (TEU)), it is for the competent national authorities to assess individual projects and to ensure compliance with EU law.

According to Article 6(3) of the Habitats Directive (1) and subject to Article 6(4), the authorities can agree to a project only after having ascertained that it will not adversely affect the integrity of the site concerned (2). Italy has transposed these provisions in its legislation (3) and adopted national guidelines (4) for their implementation. Lazio region has adopted updated guidelines and procedures (5).
The Commission has no information about a possible breach of those provisions concerning the project referred to by the Honourable Member.

Council Directive 92/43/EEC of 21 May 1992 on the conservation of natural habitats and of wild fauna and flora, OJ L 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7. See guidance document: European Commission, Directorate-General for Environment, Managing Natura 2000 sites — The provisions of Article 6 of the ‘Habitats’ Directive 92/43/EEC, Publications Office, 2019, https://data.europa.eu/doi/10.2779/02245 https://www.mase.gov.
